title: Eigen directions: when a transformation stays on a line

items.prompt: A = [[2, 1], [−1, 3]] and v = (2, 1). Using column vectors, what is Av?
Which requirement belongs to the definition of a real eigenvector v of a real matrix A?
options: v is nonzero and Av = λv for some real number λ.
v may be zero, but λ must be positive.
v must have length 1 and λ must be an integer.
v must point along a coordinate axis.

items.prompt: A nonzero vector satisfies Av = −3v. What happens to it under this one application of A?
options: It turns through a right angle.
Its length becomes negative.
It cannot be an eigenvector because the scale is negative.
Its length is multiplied by 3 and its direction reverses on the same line.

items.prompt: For A = [[1, 0], [0, 0]], the nonzero vector v = (0, 2) maps to (0, 0). Which statement is correct?
options: v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.
v is not an eigenvector because its image has no direction.
The zero output is an eigenvector with every eigenvalue.
v has eigenvalue 2 because its original length is 2.

items.prompt: Suppose Av = 2v and v is nonzero. What can be concluded about w = −4v?
options: w has eigenvalue −8.
w is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.
w is an eigenvector only if it is normalized.
w has eigenvalue −4.

items.prompt: A = [[2, 0], [0, 1]] and v = (1, 1), so Av = (2, 1). Is v an eigenvector?
options: Yes, because A is diagonal.
Yes, with eigenvalue 3.
No: no single scalar multiplies both input coordinates to produce the output.
No: eigenvectors can never have two nonzero coordinates.

items.prompt: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], the trace is 7 and determinant is 10. Which equation and pair give its eigenvalues?
For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], which pairing of eigenvector and eigenvalue is correct?
options: Both (1, 1) and (1, −1) have λ = 2.

items.prompt: A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] has the repeated eigenvalue 1. What are its real eigenvectors?
options: Every nonzero vector in the plane.
Exactly two vectors, (1, 0) and (0, 1).
All nonzero vectors on the x-axis only.
There are none because the root is repeated.

items.prompt: A = [[2, 0], [0, 2]]. How many lines through the origin consist of nonzero eigenvectors away from the origin?
options: Exactly one.
Every such line; all nonzero vectors have eigenvalue 2.
Exactly two, because the matrix is 2×2.
None, because both roots are equal.

items.prompt: A = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] rotates the real plane by 90°. Its characteristic equation is λ² + 1 = 0. What follows?
options: It has no nonzero real eigenvectors; its eigenvalues over the complex numbers are i and −i.
Its real eigenvectors are the two coordinate axes.
Its real eigenvalues are 1 and −1.
The zero vector is its only real eigenvector.

items.prompt: A = [[1, 1], [1, 0]] and v = (2, 1), so Av = (3, 2). The two arrows may look nearly aligned in a small diagram. Which exact conclusion is justified?
options: v is an eigenvector because the arrows are close.
v has eigenvalue 3/2 because the first coordinates have that ratio.
v has eigenvalue 2 because the second coordinates have that ratio.
v is not an eigenvector: 2×2 − 1×3 = 1, so the two vectors are not collinear.

items.prompt: A nonzero v satisfies Av = −2v. If the same matrix acts twice, what is A²v?
options: 4v
2v
